hints: Focus on what addition with only one reactant means, the C=C bonds must add to each other with no atoms lost or gained.
Check the formula first, each cyclohexene is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}$, so any addition dimer, trimer or polymer must keep that C to H ratio.
Compare how the rings join the chain, a true cyclohexene polymer must have the backbone carbons as part of the rings, not as a separate chain with rings hanging off.
walkthrough:
**Understand self-addition**

Cyclohexene has one C=C bond. In an addition reaction the pi bond breaks and two new sigma bonds form. If it is the only reactant, molecules of cyclohexene must add to other molecules of cyclohexene.

General idea:
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10} + \text{C}_6\text{H}_{10} + ... \rightarrow \text{addition product}$$
No other atoms are involved, so the product must contain only C and H in the same $6:10$ ratio.

**Test structure 1, the trimer**

Structure 1 shows three six-membered rings fused together. This can be built from three $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}$ molecules adding across their double bonds.

Check atoms:
$$3 \times \text{C}_6\text{H}_{10} = \text{C}_{18}\text{H}_{30}$$
The fused product still has formula $\text{C}_{18}\text{H}_{30}$. Nothing is lost, so this is a valid addition oligomer. Structure 1 is possible.

**Test structure 2, the ring-in-backbone polymer**

In addition polymerisation of a cycloalkene, the double bond in the ring opens to link to the next monomer. The two carbons that were doubly bonded become singly bonded and form the polymer backbone, but they stay inside the six-membered ring.

So the polymer looks like linked cyclohexane rings, which is exactly what structure 2 shows. The repeat unit is still $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}$. Structure 2 is possible.

**Test structure 3, the ring-on-side-chain polymer**

Structure 3 shows a separate carbon backbone with whole cyclohexyl $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}$ groups hanging off as side chains. That backbone did not come from opening a ring double bond.

That type of polymer would need a monomer like vinylcyclohexane, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH-C}_6\text{H}_{11}$, where the C=C is outside the ring. It cannot be made from cyclohexene alone. Structure 3 is not possible.

Conclusion: 1 and 2 only are possible.

options.A: This option claims 1, 2 and 3 are all possible. Structures 1 and 2 are correct, but 3 shows cyclohexane rings as pendant side groups on a separate chain. That requires an external vinyl C=C, not a ring C=C, so it cannot form from cyclohexene alone.
options.B: This option states 1 and 2 only. Structure 1 is an addition trimer with formula $\text{C}_{18}\text{H}_{30}$ and structure 2 is the correct addition polymer where the backbone carbons remain part of the rings. Both keep the $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}$ ratio with no loss of atoms.
options.C: This option claims 2 and 3 only. While 2 is correct, 3 is wrong because it is a vinyl-type polymer, and it wrongly leaves out 1, which is a valid self-addition trimer of cyclohexene.
options.D: This option claims 1 only. Structure 1 is indeed possible, but structure 2 is also possible as the normal addition polymer of cyclohexene, so limiting to 1 alone is incomplete.
